tutor:
Remember to read the requirement carefully and allocate the time spent on each section.
Part (a) covers the classic topic of tax evasion and tax avoidance, but care must be taken to
apply your knowledge to Ernest’s particular problem. This part also tests awareness of the
general anti-abuse rule.
Part (b) requires the application of common sense if the specific guidelines have not been
learnt.
Parts (c) and (d) are straightforward if the self-assessment rules have been learnt, difficult if
not learnt.
(a) Tax evasion and tax avoidance
• Tax evasion is illegal and involves the reduction of tax liabilities by not providing
information to which HMRC is entitled, or deliberately providing HMRC with
false information.
• In contrast, tax avoidance involves the minimisation of tax liabilities by the use
of any lawful means. However, certain tax avoidance schemes must be disclosed
to HMRC.
• The general anti-abuse rule is a rule to counter artificial and abusive schemes
where arrangements (which cannot be regarded as a reasonable course of
action) are put in place deliberately to avoid tax.
• If Ernest makes no disclosure of the capi tal gain then this will be viewed as tax
evasion as his tax liability for the ta x year 2025/26 will be understated by
£18,000.
(b) Failure to disclose information to HMRC
• How to deal with the failure to disclose is a matter of professional judgement,
and a trainee Chartered Certified Accountant would be expected to act honestly
and with integrity.
• Ernest should therefore be advised to disclose details of the capital gain to
HMRC.
• If such disclosure is not made by Ernest, you would be obliged to report under
the money laundering regulations, and you should also consider ceasing to act
for Ernest.
• In these circumstances you would be advised to notify HMRC that you no longer
act for him although you should not provide any reason for this.
(c) Penalties for tax agent
• A civil penalty may be payable by the firm if they have engaged in dishonest
conduct, which may be the case if they have failed to supply the information
HMRC have requested.
• The potential penalty is up to £50,000.


(d) Interest payable
• Late payment interest will run from the due date of 31 January 2027 to the
payment date of 31 July 2027.

The copyright is a wasting asset. The cost of £22,000 must therefore be depreciated based on
an unexpired life of 15 years at the date of acquisition and an unexpired life of 12 years at the
date of disposal.

The cost of the land originally purchased was for six acres but only four acres are sold. Unlike
the copyright the land is not a wasting asset, therefore the original cost must be apportioned
proportionate to the current market value. The total market value is £200,000, being
£140,000 (for the four acres sold) plus £60,000 (for the two acres not sold). Lily is also allowed
to deduct any capital costs directly relating to the sale of the four acres of land; being the
£14,400 for clearing and levelling those four acres.

The months of actual occupation are shown clearly. The deemed occupation must be
preceded and succeeded by periods of occupation so the first period of 36 months is covered
as absence for any reason (up to three years) and the second period of working elsewhere in
the UK is covered for 48 months, and the “three years for any reason” period has already been
utilised. The final period of travelling is not covered as deemed occupation since there was no
actual occupation afterwards (and the “three years for any reason” period has already been
utilised). However, nine months of the final period of ownership are covered as deemed
occupation, even if not actually occupied.

It is not necessary to calculate the allocation of cost to the shares in order to calculate the
gains, but this is shown here for completeness.

Lily’s sister has no taxable income for the year 2025/26 therefore her £37,700 basic rate band
is available. The chargeable gains (rather than taxable gains) are given and so the annual
exempt amount (AEA) is also available of £3,000. It is more beneficial to set off the AEA
against the residential gain; since residential property is subject to tax at 18% and 24%,
whereas the other gain is taxed at 14% only. However, this gain qualifying for business asset
disposal relief will use up the full basic rate band. So, this gain will be £44,200 which will be
taxed at 14%. The residential gain will be reduced by the AEA and taxed at 24%.

tutor:
Disposals of assets between married couples and civil partners are automatically on a no
gain/no loss basis. If you are provided with the market value or any actual proceeds, they are
merely there to distract you. Therefore, the gift of the house does not give rise to any gain or
loss because it is a transfer between spouses.

The gift holdover relief computation tested the restriction on gift holdover relief that applies
in a very specific scenario. When an individual makes a gift of shares in their personal
company (i.e. owns ≥5% of the shares), the gift holdover relief is restricted by reference to the
proportion of the company’s chargeable business assets to its chargeable assets.

When dealing with a part disposal of land, the market value of the part disposed and the
market value of the remainder should be used to determine the cost for the computation.
Don’t be tempted to use the proportion of asset being disposed of i.e. 9/10 hectares. The part
disposal requires the application of A/(A+B) to the full cost of the land. Any cost not included
in the computation is the base cost of the remaining land.

so it does not use any NRB at death.

tutor:
Option A describes the common inheritance tax planning technique of ‘skipping a generation’.
This technique can maximise the inheritance available to future generations as a charge to
inheritance tax will only arise once, on th e passing of the estate residue to Heng’s
grandchildren. If the residue had been left to Heng’s children and they subsequently gifted
the assets to their children, two charges to inheritance tax would arise.
That being said, skipping a generation woul d not reduce Heng’s potential inheritance tax
liability on death as legacies left to both children and grandchildren are equally chargeable.

tutor:
The loss to the donor (or diminution in value) principle applies when calculating the transfer
of value for IHT purposes. This is particularly relevant when valuing shares where a majority
shareholding has a higher value per share than a minority shareholding in a company.
The transfer of value is the amount by which Afiya’s estate has diminished and not the market
value of the asset gifted.
Prior to the transfer Afiya had 8,000 shares (an 80% (8,000/10,000) shareholding) in the
company and the shares are valued at £8 per share.
After the transfer Afiya owns 1,500 shares (a 15% shareholding) and the shares are valued at
£3 per share.

When calculating lifetime tax on a CLT, the available nil rate band is reduced by the value of
CLTs in the previous seven years. PETs are ignored for lifetime tax calculations even if they
subsequently become chargeable.

Debts are only deductible if they were outstanding at the date of death and were imposed by
law.
The £500 owed to a friend is not a debt imposed by law, and so will not be deductible.
The annual exemption is only available for deduction from lifetime gifts in the calculation of
lifetime tax. They cannot, therefore, be deducted from the death estate.

The husband did not leave a main residence to direct descendants on his death so 100% of his
residence nil rate band (RNRB) is unused and could be transferred to Afiya. Note that the
husband does not need to have died after 5 April 2017 for the RNRB to be transferred to the
surviving spouse.

As the lifetime gift was made between 1 October and 5 April in the tax year 2024/25, the due
date for the lifetime IHT on the CLT to the trust is 31 July 2025, being six months from the end
of the month in which the gift was made.
The due date for the IHT on the estate is 31 May 2026, being six months after the end of the
month in which Afiya died.

This question focuses on various aspects of IHT, including the calculation of the nil rate band,
deductible liabilities, payment responsibilities,  and tax planning implications of lifetime
transfers.
When calculating the available nil rate band, remember to consider any transferable nil rate
band from a deceased spouse. It's crucial to  apply the rules for deductible liabilities
accurately and understand how previous gifts and unused nil rate bands affect the IHT
calculation on the death estate.
Pay close attention to who is responsible for paying IHT on the death estate and the specific
due dates for such payments. Finally, when evaluating the tax savings from lifetime gifts,
compare the IHT that would have been payable if the assets were retained until death against
the actual lifetime IHT paid and any IHT still due on death as a result of the gift.

210 AURORA (ADAPTED)

Walk in the footsteps of a top tutor
examiner:
As is typical for the 10-mark question, different taxes were covered, in this case namely
inheritance tax and capital gains tax.  The question revolved around three residential
properties owned by Aurora, with two of the properties qualifying for private residence relief.
The question was not particularly technical, and much of the relevant information was
provided. However, it was important for candidates to sort out which information related to
which requirement.
• As regards inheritance tax, it was the valu es of the three properties, the amount of
outstanding interest-only mortgages, and Aurora’s main residence.
• As regards capital gains tax, it was the chargeable gains, periods of ownership and the
periods which Aurora had lived in each property.
The 10-mark question will often exclude certain reliefs. This was the case here, with both
Aurora and her deceased husba nd, Andrew, having made lifetime gifts which fully utilised
their respective inheritance tax nil rate bands of £325,000. This being the case, the nil rate
bands could simply be ignored. Only the residence nil rate bands were relevant.
The capital gains tax requirement stated that the chargeable gain should be calculated before
deducting the annual exempt amount. Therefor e, the annual exempt amount and the tax
liability were irrelevant, and could not possibly gain any marks.
With the 10-mark question, it is always a good idea for candidates to spend a few minutes
planning out their answers, especially as this can avoid wasting time taking a much longer
approach than necessary. With this requirement, the three property values and the two
mortgage figures can be combined into just the two figures – £1,050,000 (3 × £350,000 for
the property values) and £230,000 (2 × £115,000 for the mortgages). Three separate sets of
workings not only take longer, but there is more scope for error.
The next important point is that the chargeable gain figures are completely irrelevant to this
requirement, and, as already noted, so are the nil rate bands of £325,000. It is also necessary
to include the main residence valued at £500,000. This is why the reading and planning aspect
of answering the 10-mark question is so important.
The only slightly technical aspect to the requi rement is the residenc e nil rate bands. Since
Andrew is deceased and would not have used his residence nil rate band on his death (the
entire estate being left to Aurora), two residence nil rate bands of £175,000 are available.
The total of £350,000 is clearly less than the value of the main residence (£500,000). As can
be seen from the model answer, all of this is  easily combined into a computation with no
separate workings required.
Note: The question has been amended since it was originally set. Part of the examiner’s
report has been removed as it relates to a part of the question that has been deleted.
Requirement (b) – 3 marks
At just 3 marks, another short set of workings is required here.
Since the chargeable gains are given, it is just a matter of establishing the available reliefs. As
for requirement (a), it is important to ignore any information which is not relevant, such as
the property values and the mortgages.
There is a slightly more difficult aspect to this requirement:
• Although the periods of occupation are given, it is necessary to add in a further
9 months (0.75 years) where relevant for the final periods of ownership.
Note that the examiner’s comments regarding letting relief are no longer relevant due to
changes in the tax rules and have been deleted. This part of the question has been amended
to take into account the new rules.
The periods of ownership and the periods which Aurora has lived in each property are given
in years, so it makes sense to retain this format and not convert to months. The final 9 months
are simply included as 0.75 years.

within seven years of making it.
Aurora died more than five but less than six years after the date of the gift so taper relief of
60% is available. The taper relief table is given in the Tax Rates and Allowances provided in
the examination.

The residence nil rate bands can be utilised by  Aurora because her death estate includes a

Aurora has already fully utilised her nil rate  band during her lifetime and therefore none is

Examiner’s report
As is typical for the 10-mark question, different taxes were covered, in this case namely
inheritance tax and capital gains tax.  The question revolved around three residential
properties owned by Aurora, with two of the properties qualifying for private residence relief.
The question was not particularly technical, and much of the relevant information was
provided. However, it was important for candidates to sort out which information related to
which requirement.
• As regards inheritance tax, it was the valu es of the three properties, the amount of
outstanding interest-only mortgages, and Aurora’s main residence.
• As regards capital gains tax, it was the chargeable gains, periods of ownership and the
periods which Aurora had lived in each property.
The 10-mark question will often exclude certain reliefs. This was the case here, with both
Aurora and her deceased husba nd, Andrew, having made lifetime gifts which fully utilised
their respective inheritance tax nil rate bands of £325,000. This being the case, the nil rate
bands could simply be ignored. Only the residence nil rate bands were relevant.
The capital gains tax requirement stated that the chargeable gain should be calculated before
deducting the annual exempt amount. Therefor e, the annual exempt amount and the tax
liability were irrelevant, and could not possibly gain any marks.
With the 10-mark question, it is always a good idea for candidates to spend a few minutes
planning out their answers, especially as this can avoid wasting time taking a much longer
approach than necessary. With this requirement, the three property values and the two
mortgage figures can be combined into just the two figures – £1,050,000 (3 × £350,000 for
the property values) and £230,000 (2 × £115,000 for the mortgages). Three separate sets of
workings not only take longer, but there is more scope for error.
The next important point is that the chargeable gain figures are completely irrelevant to this
requirement, and, as already noted, so are the nil rate bands of £325,000. It is also necessary
to include the main residence valued at £500,000. This is why the reading and planning aspect
of answering the 10-mark question is so important.
The only slightly technical aspect to the requi rement is the residenc e nil rate bands. Since
Andrew is deceased and would not have used his residence nil rate band on his death (the
entire estate being left to Aurora), two residence nil rate bands of £175,000 are available.
The total of £350,000 is clearly less than the value of the main residence (£500,000). As can
be seen from the model answer, all of this is  easily combined into a computation with no
separate workings required.

examiner:
This question was on inheritance tax (IHT), and candidates found this to be a challenging area.
The requirement for part (a) was to calculate the IHT payable as a result of a taxpayer’s death,
and to state who was responsible for paying the tax. The taxpayer had made (1) a chargeable
lifetime transfer (more than seven years before death), (2) a potentially exempt transfer and
(3) another chargeable lifetime transfer. A quick review of the information given should have
indicated that no lifetime tax would have been paid (this fact was actually stated in respect
of the second chargeable lifetime transfer) and that taper relief was not relevant (given that
none of the gifts were between four and seven years of death). However, many candidates
dedicated a lot of time to establishing this. Candidates should read through the question
carefully before they begin their calculations.
Part (b) required an explanation as to why it might have been beneficial if the taxpayer had
left a portion of their estate to his nephew rather than to his brother. This aspect was well
answered, with most candidates appreciating the basic IHT planning of avoiding a double
charge to tax.
The IHT planning in part (c) was less well understood. It was necessary to explain why it might
be advantageous to make lifetime gifts even when such gifts are made within seven years of
death. The main advantage here is that the value of the gift is fixed at the time it is made, so
no IHT is payable on the increase in value between making the gift and the time of death.
Taper relief may also be available.

examiner:
The 10-mark higher skills question involved Jess ica, an additional rate taxpayer. On 6 April
2025, she had made a lifetime gift consisting of  both shares and cash to a trust, with the
funds then being held for the benefit of her two grandchildren aged three and four.
Although this question was well answered, the fact that the same share information had to
be used for both capital gains tax and inheritance tax purposes often caused confusion. This
is despite a similar example being included in the higher skills, chargeable gains and
inheritance tax articles. It is important to appreciate the interactions that can arise in a higher
skills question, and reading publis hed articles and practising exam standard questions will
help to this end.
Requirement (a)
The relevant information to pull out from the question is that Jessica made a gift of 100,000
£1 ordinary shares in Valuable Ltd to the trust. With Valuable Ltd having a share capital of
250,000 £1 ordinary shares, the gift represents a 40% shareholding, so the relevant deemed
proceeds figure is based on £4 per share. The shares were acquired at a £1 par value.
Therefore, the gain is simply 100,000 × £3 (£4 – £1) = £300,000 (for 2 marks). Deduct the
annual exempt amount, multiply by the higher capital gains tax rate (since Jessica is an
additional rate taxpayer), and that gives the capital gains tax figure.
Provided the valuation basis is understood, that should be a very easy and quick 3 marks.
The big problem for many candidates, of course, was that they used an inheritance tax basis
of valuation. A common error was to calculate the inheritance tax value (£900,000 – part (b))
and then deduct the correct cost figure of £100,000 (100,000 at £1). This would have wasted
a minute or two on the erroneous calculation.
Requirement (b)
The diminution in value of Jessica’s estate wa s a cash element of £250,000 (for one mark),
and the 100,000 £1 ordinary shares in Valuab le Ltd. Before the transfer, Jessica owned
150,000 shares; a 60% shareholding valued at £7 per share. After the transfer, Jessica owned
50,000 shares; a 20% shareholding valued at £3 per share. The diminution in value from the
gift of shares was therefore (150,000 at £7) – (50,000 at £3) = £900,000 (for 2 marks).

The total value of the transfer was therefore £1,150,000 (£250,000 + £900,000). It was then
just a case of deducting the full nil rate band of £325,000, with lifetime tax calculated at the
rate of 20% (since the trust paid the inheritance tax arising).
This requirement was quite well answered, although a very common mistake was to exclude
the £50,000 held within cash ISAs from the cash element of £250,000. Even though the
requirement was to ignore the inheritance tax annual exemption, quite a few candidates still
deducted this. Despite the scenario clearly stating that the trust paid the inheritance tax
arising, a number of candidates grossed up the tax due using a rate of 20/80ths.
Requirement (c)
The gift impacted on Jessica’s savings income and her dividend income.
Savings income: If the gift had not been made, Jessica would have received savings income
of £6,250 on the cash held during the tax year, of which £1,250 would have been from ISAs.
Dividend income: If the gift had not been made, Jessica would have had dividend income of
£24,000. This was reduced to £8,000 as a result of making the gift of shares.
There were many perfect answers to this requirement, although answers were often more
complicated than they needed to be.
Savings income: The ISA intere st was not relevant (being exempt), so the income tax
reduction was simply £5,000 (£6,250 – £1,250) at 45% = £2,250 for 1.5 marks. Any attempt
to include the personal allowance made it impossible to score full marks.
Dividend income: Here, the income tax reduction was £16,000 (£24,000 – £8,000) at 39.35%
= £6,296 for 1.5 marks. The dividend nil rate band often caused unnecessary complications,
although full marks were still available if the nil rate band was deducted from both ‘before
gift’ and ‘after gift’ computations.
Candidates should be careful to use the correct tax rates which are clearly shown in the tax
tables available in the exam.

Examiner’s report
The 10-mark higher skills question involved Jess ica, an additional rate taxpayer. On 6 April
2025, she had made a lifetime gift consisting of  both shares and cash to a trust, with the
funds then being held for the benefit of her two grandchildren aged three and four.
Although this question was well answered, the fact that the same share information had to
be used for both capital gains tax and inheritance tax purposes often caused confusion. This
is despite a similar example being included in the higher skills, chargeable gains and
inheritance tax articles. It is important to appreciate the interactions that can arise in a higher
skills question, and reading publis hed articles and practising exam standard questions will
help to this end.
Requirement (a)
The relevant information to pull out from the question is that Jessica made a gift of 100,000
£1 ordinary shares in Valuable Ltd to the trust. With Valuable Ltd having a share capital of
250,000 £1 ordinary shares, the gift represents a 40% shareholding, so the relevant deemed
proceeds figure is based on £4 per share. The shares were acquired at a £1 par value.
Therefore, the gain is simply 100,000 × £3 (£4 – £1) = £300,000 (for 2 marks). Deduct the
annual exempt amount, multiply by the higher capital gains tax rate (since Jessica is an
additional rate taxpayer), and that gives the capital gains tax figure.
Provided the valuation basis is understood, that should be a very easy and quick 3 marks.
The big problem for many candidates, of course, was that they used an inheritance tax basis
of valuation. A common error was to calculate the inheritance tax value (£900,000 – part (b))
and then deduct the correct cost figure of £100,000 (100,000 at £1). This would have wasted
a minute or two on the erroneous calculation.
Requirement (b)
The diminution in value of Jessica’s estate wa s a cash element of £250,000 (for one mark),
and the 100,000 £1 ordinary shares in Valuab le Ltd. Before the transfer, Jessica owned
150,000 shares; a 60% shareholding valued at £7 per share. After the transfer, Jessica owned
50,000 shares; a 20% shareholding valued at £3 per share. The diminution in value from the
gift of shares was therefore (150,000 at £7) – (50,000 at £3) = £900,000 (for 2 marks).

The total value of the transfer was therefore £1,150,000 (£250,000 + £900,000). It was then
just a case of deducting the full nil rate band of £325,000, with lifetime tax calculated at the
rate of 20% (since the trust paid the inheritance tax arising).
This requirement was quite well answered, although a very common mistake was to exclude
the £50,000 held within cash ISAs from the cash element of £250,000. Even though the
requirement was to ignore the inheritance tax annual exemption, quite a few candidates still
deducted this. Despite the scenario clearly stating that the trust paid the inheritance tax
arising, a number of candidates grossed up the tax due using a rate of 20/80ths.
Requirement (c)
The gift impacted on Jessica’s savings income and her dividend income.
Savings income: If the gift had not been made, Jessica would have received savings income
of £6,250 on the cash held during the tax year, of which £1,250 would have been from ISAs.
Dividend income: If the gift had not been made, Jessica would have had dividend income of
£24,000. This was reduced to £8,000 as a result of making the gift of shares.
There were many perfect answers to this requirement, although answers were often more
complicated than they needed to be.
Savings income: The ISA intere st was not relevant (being exempt), so the income tax
reduction was simply £5,000 (£6,250 – £1,250) at 45% = £2,250 for 1.5 marks. Any attempt
to include the personal allowance made it impossible to score full marks.
Dividend income: Here, the income tax reduction was £16,000 (£24,000 – £8,000) at 39.35%
= £6,296 for 1.5 marks. The dividend nil rate band often caused unnecessary complications,
although full marks were still available if the nil rate band was deducted from both ‘before
gift’ and ‘after gift’ computations.
Candidates should be careful to use the correct tax rates which are clearly shown in the tax
tables available in the exam.

tutor:
A large company is required to pay its final instalment of corporation tax by the 14th day of
the 4th month after the end of the accounting period (AP). Note that for a 12-month AP this
is 16 months after the start of the AP.
Where an AP is less than 12 months, the first instalment is due by the 14th day of the
7th month after the start of the AP. Subsequent instalments are due at 3 monthly intervals
thereafter, until the date of the final instalment is reached.
For an eight-month AP instalments are due on the 14th day of months 7, 10 and 12 (the last
being 4 months after the end of the AP). For this scenario, that is 14  July 2025, 14 October
2025 and 14 December 2025.
The first two instalments are calculated as 3/8 × corporation tax liability (£400,000 × 3/8 =
£150,000). The final instalment will be 2/8 × corporation tax liability.

tutor:
Two companies are associated companies if:
– One of the companies is under the control of the other, or
– Both are under the control of the same person or persons.
Control is where more than 50% of the ordinary share capital is directly or indirectly owned.
It does not matter where a company is resident so overseas companies are included in the
definition.

Your first step should be to identify which companies are in a group relief group with
Deutsch Ltd. You can then identify how much group relief is available.
• Deutsch Ltd cannot claim group relief from Eins Ltd as this company is not a 75%
subsidiary. However, Drei Ltd and Deutsch Ltd are in a group relief group.
• The maximum amount of group relief that can be claimed is £64,700 being
Drei Ltd’s trading loss of £52,700 plus  the unrelieved qualifying charitable
donations of £12,000.

• The surrendering company may surrender any amount of its current period losses.
• There is no requirement for the surrendering company to relieve the loss against its
own profits first.
• The current period losses which may be surrendered are trading losses, unrelieved
QCDs and unrelieved property losses.

Where there is only partial reinvestment of the proceeds on disposal, the amount that has not
been reinvested is immediately chargeable to tax. The balance of the indexed gain can be
rolled over into the purchase of the new asset.

Berlin Ltd owns more than 75% of Zwei Ltd. The two companies therefore form a group for
capital gains purposes.
Assets transferred within a gains group are automatically transferred at no gain/no loss
(i.e. without a chargeable gain or allowable loss arising).
The transfer is deemed to take place at a price that does not give rise to a gain or a loss
(i.e. the indexed cost at the date of the transfer).
The transferor’s deemed proceeds figure is also the deemed cost of the acquiring company.

The claim for group relief must be made by Deutsch Ltd (the claimant company) on its
corporation tax return by 31 March 2028 (within two years of the end of the accounting period
when the loss is group relieved).
The claim for rollover relief must be made within four years of the end accounting period in
which the assets are sold and replaced (whichever is later) i.e. 31 March 2030 in this scenario.

Time limits for claims and elections should represent easy marks provided that you have learnt
them prior to the examination.

appreciate that there was an accounting period running from 1 October 2025 to 28 February
2026, or they had just the one period running from 1 May 2025 to 28 February 2026.
Requirement (b) – 9 marks
With this type of answer containing additions and deductions, candidates should be careful
to indicate which is which. A single column approach with deductions included as such on the
spreadsheet avoids any confusion. It is then just a matter of using the SUM function to get to
a figure for taxable total profits. Candidates who added up their total figure on a cell-by-cell
basis (e.g. A1 + A2 + A3 etc) invariably had problems when it came to negative entries, and it
was sometimes difficult for markers to determine whether a figure was a plus or a minus.
None of the adjustments or entries really needed separate workings. The capital allowances
were simply £220,000 at 100%, and £30,000 at 18% (for one mark in each case), and the gain
was calculated as the proceeds of £204,000 less the reinvestment of £168,000 (1.5 marks).
This requirement was generally very well answ ered. The only aspects which consistently
caused problems were the two interest figures and the chargeable gain. It was somewhat
surprising to see a number of candidates adding the figure for interest payable and deducting
the figure for interest receivable. Such carelessness cost a half mark in each case.
With the chargeable gain, it was clearly stated that Elara Ltd had made a claim to rollover the
gain, so this should have represented a fairly easy 1.5 marks.
Many candidates forgot to make the deduction for the qualifying charitable donations, even
where they had correctly added them back earlier in their computation.
Requirement (c) – 4 marks
There were quite a number of perfect answers to this requirement, although a number of
candidates did not appreciate that payment of a dividend and the advance rental payment
would not impact Fenrir Ltd’s corporation tax liability for year ending 31 March 2026. This is
because dividends are paid out of post-tax profits, and (given the accruals basis of accounts
preparation) rent paid in advance would not be deductible for the year ended 31 March 2026.
Having worked out the adjustments, candidates then needed to calculate the tax saving. This
could either be done by multiplying the adjustment by the corporation tax rate of 25%, or
working out a revised corporation tax liability and comparing this to the previous liability.
Well prepared candidates were able to answer this requirement quickly (a benefit of question
practice), scoring a fairly straightforward four marks and saving time. However, a correct
answer for the car – along with the 25% tax saving – was sufficient to score half of the marks.

Examiner’s report
The question was generally very well answered, with many candidates scoring high marks.
The question involved three unrelated companies; Deimos Ltd, Elara Ltd and Fenrir Ltd.
Requirement (a) – 2 marks
There was one mark for the period 1 May 2024 to  30 April 2025, a half mark for the period
1 May 2025 to 30 September 2025 (the period of account to 30 September 2025 being split
into two accounting periods), and a half mark for the period from 1 October 2025 (from the
date of the final financial statements) to 28 February 2026 (completion of winding up).
This requirement was generally well answered, although many candidates either did not
appreciate that there was an accounting period running from 1 October 2025 to 28 February
2026, or they had just the one period running from 1 May 2025 to 28 February 2026.
Requirement (b) – 9 marks
With this type of answer containing additions and deductions, candidates should be careful
to indicate which is which. A single column approach with deductions included as such on the
spreadsheet avoids any confusion. It is then just a matter of using the SUM function to get to
a figure for taxable total profits. Candidates who added up their total figure on a cell-by-cell
basis (e.g. A1 + A2 + A3 etc) invariably had problems when it came to negative entries, and it
was sometimes difficult for markers to determine whether a figure was a plus or a minus.
None of the adjustments or entries really needed separate workings. The capital allowances
were simply £220,000 at 100%, and £30,000 at 18% (for one mark in each case), and the gain
was calculated as the proceeds of £204,000 less the reinvestment of £168,000 (1.5 marks).
This requirement was generally very well answ ered. The only aspects which consistently
caused problems were the two interest figures and the chargeable gain. It was somewhat
surprising to see a number of candidates adding the figure for interest payable and deducting
the figure for interest receivable. Such carelessness cost a half mark in each case.
With the chargeable gain, it was clearly stated that Elara Ltd had made a claim to rollover the
gain, so this should have represented a fairly easy 1.5 marks.
Many candidates forgot to make the deduction for the qualifying charitable donations, even
where they had correctly added them back earlier in their computation.
Requirement (c) – 4 marks
There were quite a number of perfect answers to this requirement, although a number of
candidates did not appreciate that payment of a dividend and the advance rental payment
would not impact Fenrir Ltd’s corporation tax liability for year ending 31 March 2026. This is
because dividends are paid out of post-tax profits, and (given the accruals basis of accounts
preparation) rent paid in advance would not be deductible for the year ended 31 March 2026.
Having worked out the adjustments, candidates then needed to calculate the tax saving. This
could either be done by multiplying the adjustment by the corporation tax rate of 25%, or
working out a revised corporation tax liability and comparing this to the previous liability.
Well prepared candidates were able to answer this requirement quickly (a benefit of question
practice), scoring a fairly straightforward four marks and saving time. However, a correct
answer for the car – along with the 25% tax saving – was sufficient to score half of the marks.

examiner:
The corporation tax question was generally very well answered, with many candidates
scoring high marks.
Requirement (a) – 15 marks
Commencing with the operating profit, candidates were required to adjust for the following:
Disallowable expenditure (2.5 marks): There were five items to consider, and these were all
non-allowable. The majority of candidates correctly adjusted for four or five of the items,
although the amortisation and/or the qualif ying charitable donations were sometimes
missed. For this style of question, it is very important that candidates clearly indicate whether
items are being added or deducted. A single column layout is therefore recommended.
Leasehold premium (3 marks):  Many candidates had no difficulty calculating the correct
deduction for the grant of a 12-year lease. One common mistake, however, was to work out
the non-chargeable portion of the lease (£96,000 × 2% × (12 – 1) = £21,120) and then use
that for the basis of the lease deduction rather than working out the chargeable portion
(£96,000 – £21,120 = £74,880). Although most candidates appreciated that the chargeable
portion then had to be divided by the number of years of the lease (12 years), quite a few did
not then apply the 6/12ths restriction; the lease being granted on 1 October 2025.
An alternative approach to calculating the chargeable portion of the lease was £96,000 × (51
– 12)/50 = £74,880. If using this approach, candidates needed to take care as the incorrect
number of years (51 years and 12 years) were often used.
It was also important to realise that the final result had to be deducted in the main
computation.
Regardless of approach, it is not recommended to attempt the entire working within the one
spreadsheet cell. For example, missing the brackets on £96,000 × 51 – 12/50 would give an
answer of £4,896,000. Provided the correct wo rkings are shown, appropriate marks will be
awarded even if a candidate makes an arithmetical error. Without workings, it can be difficult
determining what the candidate’s intention is.
Capital allowances (5.5 marks):  There were quite a lot of marks for a capital allowances
computation, so care was needed. It was pleasing to see many perfect answers, but some
candidates struggled here. It was necessary to decide whether an asset purchase qualified
for the 100% annual investment allowance, and, if not qualifying , whether the purchase went
into the main pool or the special rate pool.
The aspect which caused most difficulty was the disposal of the car purchased during the
same year. The correct treatment was to add the addition and to deduct the disposal
proceeds from the special rate pool. However, many candidates kept this car separate and
calculated a balancing adjustment.
Other income (2 marks):  The other income consisted of bank interest (it was necessary to
add in a year end accrual), dividends from an 80% UK subsidiary company (this was exempt
income) and a chargeable gain (the profit before taking account of the indexation allowance
was also given).
Once again, there were a lot of perfect answers here. Typical mistakes included deducting
the bank interest accrual, treating the dividend as taxable, and using the pre-indexed gain or
deducting the annual exempt amount of £3,000. This is why question practice is so important
because these are the type of mistakes which if made once, are less likely to be repeated.

Deductions (1.5 marks):  After adding it back to trading profits earlier, the qualifying
charitable donation now had to be deducted from total profits for a half mark. A group relief
deduction was also available in respect of a trading loss made by the 80% UK subsidiary
company. There was one mark for this, but only a half mark if not deducted at the correct
point in the main computation or if the loss was restricted to 80%.
Corporation tax (0.5 mark):  The final mark was for calculating the corporation tax liability.
This generally wasn’t a problem, although a few candidates kept the chargeable gain separate
and then applied a different rate of tax on this. [Note that when this question was originally
set there was only one rate of corporation tax and this calculation was for only half a mark.]
As already mentioned, with computations containing both additions and deductions,
candidates should be very careful to indicate which is which. A single column approach with
deductions included as such on the spreadsheet avoids any confusion. It is then just a matter
of using the SUM function to get to a figure fo r taxable total profits. The simplicity of this
approach is that the same layout can be used regardless of whether a profit or a loss is
involved.
The only aspects of the answer which warranted separate workings were the leasehold
premium and the capital allowances. Everything else was easily dealt with within the main
computation.
Layout is not something candidates should really be concerned about on the day. With
sufficient question practice, the correct layout becomes automatic.

Being able to determine when corporation tax is payable is a common examination
requirement, and it is important to learn the rules about which companies must pay by
quarterly instalments and the exceptions from that system, which are relevant here.
• Large companies have to make quarterly instalment payments in respect of their
corporation tax liability. A large comp any is one with augmented profits
exceeding £1,500,000, adjusted for sh ort accounting periods and associated
companies.
• However, a company is not required to make quarterly instalment payments in
the first year that it is large.
Therefore, E-Commerce plc will not have been required to make instalment
payments for the year ended 31 March 2026 as it was not a large company in
the year ended 31 March 2025.
This is because the augmented profits of £1,360,000 were less than £1,500,000.
• For the year ended 31 March 2027, this exception will not apply. Therefore,
E-Commerce plc will have to make quarterly instalment payments as its
augmented profits will exceed £1,500,000.

examiner:
The corporation tax question was very well answered, with many candidates scoring high
marks. The question required candidates to calculate Cop Ltd’s trading loss and taxable total
profits for the three-month period 1 October to 31 December.
As for the income tax question, there were various ways of approaching this question. Again,
the easiest one was to have a main computation working out the trading loss, with this then
extended to include the chargeable gain and qualifying charitable donation to arrive at a
figure for taxable total profits. Capital allowances and the chargeable gain both warranted
separate workings.
In regard to the main computation, there were two issues which sometimes caused
problems:
• Candidates were instructed to indicate by the use of zero (0) any items which did not
require adjustment. There were in fact five items of expenditure where no adjustment
was required (because they were allowable), representing a total of 2.5 marks. A
number of candidates did not do as instructed and therefore would not have gained
these very easy 2.5 marks even if the remainder of their workings were correct.
Remember it is important to read and follow the instructions given in the requirement.
• With this type of answer containing both additions and deductions, candidates should
be very careful to indicate which is which. A single column approach with deductions
shown clearly as such on the spreadsheet avoids any confusion. Those candidates who
did not show the deductions clearly invariably had problems when it came to showing
totals with negative entries, and it was sometimes difficult for markers to determine
whether a figure was a plus or a minus.
One other point to bear in mind is that candidates should answer a question in the order in
which information is provided. The information was provided in the order (1) donations, (2)
legal and professional fees, (3) promotional costs and (4) annual party. So, adjustments
should follow the same sequence. If this a pproach is followed, it allows markers the
opportunity to sometimes award a mark where an obvious mistake has been made.
Capital allowances
The fact that the accounting period was only three months long meant care had to be taken
with the capital allowances working:
• The £1,000,000 annual investment allowance expenditure limit was £1,000,000 × 3/12
= £250,000.
• There was no restriction in regard to first-year allowances.
• The 18% and 6% writing down allowances were both restricted by 3/12ths.
Despite these complications, quite a number of candidates correctly calculated the capital
allowances figure for 5 marks, with many achieving 4 or 4.5 marks.
The main problem was with the car in the specia l rate pool which was bought (for £57,000)
and sold (for £50,000) during the accounting period. Despite this being the only asset in the
special rate pool, there was not a balancing adjustment, but, instead, a writing down
allowance calculated as normal.

Chargeable gain
The chargeable gain was probably the most difficult aspect of this question, especially as two
separate indexation allowance workings were necessary.
• The incidental costs had to be picked up from the disallowance of legal and
professional fees. This figure was then deducted from the disposal proceeds, so was
not relevant when it came to the indexation allowance calculations.
• One surprising mistake was sometimes the indexation allowances were calculated, but
then only those figures deducted and not the cost and enhancement expenditure
figures on which the indexation allowances were based.
Candidates should particularly note that the annual exempt amount is NOT relevant to
corporation tax.

relieve its trading loss, property business loss and capital loss. Provided candidates

for a loss incurred in the early years of a trade.

allowances as another negative. This is then consistent with a profit adjustment question
commencing with a profit, avoiding the loss of some easy marks if negatives and positives
are confused. The total can then be obtained using the SUM function on the spreadsheet.
Some candidates showed all figures as positive and then tried to calculate the total within
the cell on the lines of – A1+A2+A3-A4. It is also very easy to make mistakes using this
approach.

worryingly, confused income and corporation taxes.

on disposal of shares) was relevant to this part of the question since the requirement was
just to calculate the tax adjusted trading loss.

Examiner’s report
The corporation tax question was generally quite well answered, although (somewhat
surprisingly) the capital allowances working in part (b) caused problems. Candidates often
ended up with a reasonably correct answer to part (c)(i), where loss relief was claimed, but
spent a lot of time on irrelevant workings in reaching that point.
One common problem seen in part (b) was the inability to deal with negatives. The
requirement was to calculate Mooncake Ltd's tax adjusted trading loss, commencing with
the operating loss figure of £93,820. This meant that the adjustments for non-allowable
expenditure reduced the amount of loss, but the loss was increased by capital allowances.
As shown in the suggested solution, the easies t approach was to start with £93,820 as a
negative figure, show non-allowable expenditure as positive figures and then include capital
allowances as another negative. This is then consistent with a profit adjustment question
commencing with a profit, avoiding the loss of some easy marks if negatives and positives
are confused. The total can then be obtained using the SUM function on the spreadsheet.
Some candidates showed all figures as positive and then tried to calculate the total within
the cell on the lines of – A1+A2+A3-A4. It is also very easy to make mistakes using this
approach.
The only aspect requiring a separate working was one for capital allowances.
Requirement (a)
Although many candidates easily picked up the [three] available marks, many instead wrote
at length about available loss reliefs.
The fact that this requirement is just for [3] marks, together with the use of ‘state’ should be
a very good indication that only a short set of answers is required. This is why it is important
to make use of the model answers since candidates’ answers should, ideally, not be any
longer than those.
Candidates who mentioned loss of personal allowances or annual exempt amounts had,
worryingly, confused income and corporation taxes.
Requirement (b)
When answering this type of question, candidates are advised to answer in the same order
as information is presented. So here, the first item was depreciation, and that, therefore,
should have been the first adjustment. This approach makes it easier for markers to follow a
candidate’s answer, and there is less scope for missing out any of the adjustments.
As can be seen from the suggested solution, the capital allowances working was fairly
straightforward, involving just a main pool. There were three disposal figures to deduct from
the brought forward written down value, with an 18% writing down allowance calculated on
the remaining balance. The only reason for pr oviding the cost figures was so that (where
relevant) proceeds could be restricted to original cost. However, many candidates included
the cost figures as additions, and there were then various permutations involving balancing
adjustments. Again, this is why question practice is so important.
It should also be noted that none of the other information (property business loss and profit
on disposal of shares) was relevant to this part of the question since the requirement was
just to calculate the tax adjusted trading loss.

Requirement (c)(i)
With only losses for the year ended 31 March 2026, there was obviously no income. However,
this should have been indicated by the use of zeros (0). There was no chargeable gain because
the indexation allowance of £6,700 exceeded the gain of £3,700. This did not create a loss,
and there was no need to utilise the capital loss brought forward from the year ended
31 March 2025. These were both common mistakes made by candidates.
Another common mistake was to carry back the property business loss. Many candidates
assumed that the qualifying charitable donations for the year ended 31 March 2025 were
wasted despite the trading loss being considerably less than income. The suggested solution
shows how it is much easier to lay out this type of answer using a two-column approach with
one column for each year. Although most candi dates did reasonably well in this part, there
were not many perfect answers.
Requirement (c)(ii)
Although marks were awarded based on what candidates had done in part (c)(i), the need to
carry out an overall review and see what was left appeared to be challenging for many
candidates. The correct answer was that there was an unused capital loss from the year
ended 31 March 2025, and a property business loss from the year ended 31 March 2026. For
full marks, it was also necessary to show that the trading loss had been fully utilised, and that
the unused qualifying charitable donations from the year ended 31 March 2026 were wasted.
So four points for a half-mark each, and what should have been a very short answer.
There were very few perfect answers, with many candidates picking up just one or two half-
marks and wasting time on unnecessary detailed workings.
The use of ‘calculate’ in the requirement should have indicated that no explanation was
necessary.

In this question there are ten marks for written explanations of the gains group and
associated company rules. It is important to st ate the basic rule and then apply to the facts
of the question. Be careful with the overseas company, which is included but unable to enjoy
the benefits of gains group status.
The highlighted words in the answer are key phrases that markers are looking for.


(a) Capital gains group
• Companies form a capital gains group if at  each level in the group structure there
is a 75% shareholding, provided the parent company has an effective interest of
more than 50%.
• Alto Ltd, Bass Ltd, Cello Ltd, Echo Inc and Flute Ltd are all 75% subsidiaries, and
Music plc has an effective interest of 60% (80% × 75%) in Flute Ltd. All of these
companies therefore form a capital gains group.
• However, Bass Ltd and Cello Ltd will only be included in respect of assets
acquired or disposed of whilst they were members of the group.
• Drum Ltd and Gong Ltd are not included as Drum Ltd is not a 75% subsidiary,
and Music plc’s effective interest in Gong Ltd is only 48% (80% × 75% × 80%).
• Although Echo Inc is included in the definition of the capital gains group,
companies that are resident overseas are not able to take advantage of the
provisions applicable to a capital gains group.
(b) Associated companies
• Alto Ltd, Bass Ltd, Cello Ltd, Echo In c, Flute Ltd and Gong Ltd are all under the
common control of Music plc, and are therefore associated companies.
• Companies associated for part of the accounting period, such as Bass Ltd and
Cello Ltd, count as associated companies for the whole of the period.
• For these purposes, it does not matter where a company is resident. Echo Inc is
therefore included despite being resident overseas.
• Drum Ltd is not included as an associated company since Music plc’s effective
interest in this company is only 45%.

examiner:
The corporation tax question was fairly well answered, although many candidates had
difficulty when it came to requirement (b).
Along with a trading profit, for the year ended 31 March 2026 Maximum Ltd had property
business income and chargeable  gains. The company made qualifying charitable donations
and political donations during the year. Maximum Ltd had brought forward amounts of
trading loss, property business loss and capital loss.
Maximum Ltd had two subsidiary companies. Xim Ltd was a 75% group company, whereas
Mum Ltd (with a 65% shareholding) was not.
Requirement (a)
One important point to appreciate is that property business income and chargeable gains are
both included within the calculation of taxable total profits (TTP), yet a number of candidates
kept these elements entirely separate from the trading profit (even though all income and
gains form part of the TTP).
The starting point was to adjust the trading profit for three items:
Leasehold premium deduction (1.5 marks): The essential point to appreciate here was that
the figure provided was the amount of premium assessed on the landlord (£22,320), and not
the amount of premium itself. Therefore, the first step in the calculation had already been
done. The relevant deduction was simply the assessed amount divided by the number of years
of the lease (8 years), with an 8/12ths restriction; the lease being granted on 1 August 2025.
It was also important to realise that the final result (22,320/8 × 8/12 = £1,860) had to be
deducted in the main computation, not added.
Leasing costs disallowance (1.5 marks): Leasing costs for two cars had been deducted in
arriving at the trading profit. The first car had CO2 emissions of 40 grams per kilometre, so no
adjustment was required. The second car had CO 2 emissions in excess of 50 grams per
kilometre, so a 15% add-back was required. This adjustment often caused problems, with
various mistakes made. For example, sometimes the 15% add-back was applied for both cars,
or adjustment was made for the 85% deductible element of the leasing costs for the second
car.
Deduction for employee bonuses (1 mark): Bonuses of £20,000 were paid on 30 November
2026, with a further £16,000 paid on 15 February 2027. No entitlement to the bonuses arose
until the time that they were paid. The essential point here is that only the bonuses paid
within nine months of the end of maximum Ltd’s period of account are deductible, so not
those paid on 15 February 2027.
Having calculated a revised trading profit figure, the next steps were to calculate the property
business income and chargeable gains:
Property business income (3 marks):  This was a fairly straightforward computation for
3 marks based around a freehold warehouse which was let for a seven-month period before
the warehouse was subsequently sold. There were many perfect answers. Some candidates
struggled with the insurance payment, often trying to restrict this to the period the
warehouse was let out or owned by Maximum Ltd. However, it should have been obvious
that this aspect was taken into account due to Maximum Ltd receiving a refund of the
insurance premium paid. The correct deduction was therefore simply the insurance premium
paid (£1,320) less the refund (£190).

Chargeable gains (3 marks):  The chargeable gains computation was somewhat more
complicated, although there were still a number of perfect answers. Some candidates did not
appreciate that they had been given the two relevant chargeable gain figures (a freehold
factory was sold as well as the freehold warehouse), so no chargeable gain calculations were
required. However, the gain on the disposal of the factory could be rolled over (the proceeds
being fully reinvested – and that is why proc eed figures were provided). The gain on the
disposal of the warehouse could not be rolled over because this property was not used for
business purposes. It was also necessary to deduct the brought forward capital loss as this
was automatically relieved (however, the mark available was given even if this deduction was
made in the answer to requirement (b)).
Donations (1 mark): Finally, it was a matter of deducting the qualifying charitable donations,
and indicating (by the use of a zero) that no deduction was available for the political
donations; many candidates missed an easy half mark by not showing this zero, despite being
instructed to do so.
As already mentioned, with computations containing both additions and deductions,
candidates should be very careful to indicate which is which. A single column approach with
deductions shown clearly as such on the spreadsheet avoids any confusion.
It is best to avoid putting workings for two or three marks within the one cell, which is what
some candidates did with their business property income calculation. It is very easy to make
mistakes, and workings have to be clearly shown in order for marks to be awarded.
Requirement (b)
This requirement caused a lot of problems. Even if answering correctly, candidates often took
a very long-winded approach towards a final answer, wasting considerable time in the
process. Also, with what were often a half page of notes and workings, it was sometimes
difficult to find a candidate’s final answer.
As already mentioned, Maximum Ltd had brought forward amounts of trading loss
(£288,200) and property business loss (£3,800). The brought forward capital loss should have
been set against the chargeable gain, and is therefore irrelevant to this requirement.
Simply taking the brought forward trading loss and using this against the (candidate’s own
figure) taxable total profits of Maximum Ltd for the year ended 31 March 2026 scored
1.5 marks. Add in the brought forward property business loss, and that scored half the
available marks.
The other two marks were for dealing with the group relief aspects. One problem here,
however, was that some candidates got into considerable confusion by treating the trading
profits of the two subsidiary companies instead as trading losses. The correct treatment was
to offset the brought forward trading loss against the trading profit of Xim Ltd (£21,400), and
then to show or state that no relief was av ailable against the profits of Mum Ltd. Many
candidates – despite correctly dealing with Xim Ltd – did not mention Mum Ltd.

£288,200 + £3,800 – own figure taxable total profits – £21,400 – £0.

Voluntary registration is beneficial for traders who can recover their input VAT and either
make zero rated supplies (so will not have to charge higher prices inclusive of VAT), or make
supplies to other VAT registered businesses (who can recover the additional cost of the
output VAT charged).
A business which buys zero rated supplies and sells standard rated goods to members of the
public, will not benefit by voluntary registration since it will not recover VAT on its purchases
(as these have no VAT being zero rated) and will have to charge members of the public an
extra 20% to recover the VAT on sales.
A business which buys zero rated supplies and sells zero rated goods to members of the
public will not benefit from voluntary registration as there is no VAT to be charged on sales
or recovered on expenses.

tutor:
There are multiple separate requirements here – to advise of the penalty implications of a
further late submission; to advise of the penalty and interest implications of a further late
payment and to state what the company needs to do to avoid future penalties.  You must
make sure you deal with each requirement and give four clear points to get the four marks
available.
Penalties are tested relatively frequently. The key points to grasp are that there is no penalty
for late submission until the business has four penalty points, but once it has four points,
penalties are payable on each subsequent late submission until the points revert to zero.
The amount of the penalty needs to be learnt as they are not included in the Tax Rates and
Allowances provided in the examination.
And to avoid further penalties, the company will need to submit 4 consecutive returns on time.
In respect of late payment of VAT, both interest and penalties may be payable.  The details of
these are provided in your tax tables.
• Tardy plc has already got three penalty points, so a late submission of the next
return will result in four penalty poin ts and therefore a penalty of £200 being
charged.
• VAT being paid more than 30 days late will result in a penalty of 6% of the
overdue VAT, plus a daily penalty at an annual rate of 10%.
• Late payment interest will also be charged at 8.5% for the period until the VAT
is paid.
• In order to avoid future penalties, Tard y plc will need to submit four consecutive
VAT returns on time, the penalty points will then revert to zero.


(b) Supply of services

This part also has two requirements, when and how the VAT should be accounted for. It would
be easy to miss the first part of this requirement, which is actually about tax points, rather
than overseas supplies. Note that the question relates to services, not goods, and therefore
the tax point rules are different.
The second requirement requires an explanation of the reverse charge procedure, by which
VAT is accounted for in the country where the services are carried out.
• VAT should be accounted for on the earliest of the date when the service is
completed, the date the service is paid for, and the date the invoice is issued.
• Output VAT at the UK VAT rate should be declared on the UK business’s VAT
return.
This will then be reclaimed as input VAT on the same VAT return, so the effect
will be VAT neutral.
This is known as the reverse charge procedure.
(c) Errors on a VAT return

The requirement here is to explain why the error can be disclosed on the next return, which
means applying the de minimis test to the amount of the error. Since the error is less than
£10,000, the company’s turnover figure is not required.
• Tardy plc will be permitted to disclose  the underpayment of VAT of £8,200 by
entering this amount on its next VAT return as the net error is less than the limit
of £10,000.


(d) VAT penalties

This question covers the standard penalty for an incorrect return. The same penalty system
applies to income tax, NICs, corporation tax and VAT and could be tested in relation to any of
those taxes. Note that the penalties for errors are included in the Tax Rates and Allowances
provided in the examination.
Here you are asked for the maximum amount of the penalty, which depends upon the
taxpayer’s behaviour and also by how much it could be reduced by an unprompted disclosure.
Again, make sure you cover both points in your answer.
• Tardy plc has been careless in its incorrect treatment of the supply of services
received, so the maximum amount of penalty will therefore be 30% of the VAT
underpaid (£8,200 × 30% = £2,460).
• However, this penalty could be reduced to £0 as a result of the company’s
unprompted disclosure to HM Revenue & Customs.

This requirement has two parts (joining and leaving the flat rate scheme), so be sure that you
address both parts.
• Zia can join the flat rate scheme from 1 April 2026 because his taxable turnover
(excluding VAT) for the next 12 months is not expected to exceed £150,000.
• He can continue to use the scheme until his total turnover (including VAT, but
excluding sales of capital assets) for the previous year exceeds £230,000.

It is also necessary to leave the flat scheme if  total turnover is expected to exceed £230,000
during the following 30 days.
Although candidates are not expected to be aware of this point, equivalent marks were
awarded if this was given instead of the previous year limit.


(c) Flat rate scheme – benefits

The notes underneath the requirement give a strong hint to recalculate the liability using the
flat rate given. Remember to then conclude whether or not it would have been beneficial to
have used the scheme.
• Using the flat rate scheme to calculate his VAT liability, Zia would have paid VAT
of £15,120 (£126,000 × 12%) for the year ended 31 March 2026.
• It would therefore not have been beneficial to use the flat rate scheme as the
additional cost of £6,260 (£15,120 – £8,860) for the year would appear to
outweigh the advantage of simplified VAT administration.

Under the flat rate scheme Zia would be required to pay the flat rate percentage of his VAT-
inclusive turnover (including zero-rated supplies) with no deductions for input VAT.
